children.name: Teacher Planning, Grading, and Feedback
children.blurb: Fifteen teachers in five primary schools in England used AI to help plan lessons for two school terms. Their self reported weekly planning time fell by 52.5 percent, from about 10 hours to under 5 (Carson et al., 2026).

children.name: Assessment, Data, and the Early Warning System
children.blurb: Researchers who build systems to predict student failure found something troubling when they looked closely. A single accuracy number made predictions look more reliable than they were.

children.name: Operations, Facilities, Transportation, and Finance
children.blurb: Boston Public Schools once faced a transportation problem that cost more than $100 million a year. Researchers built an optimization system that redesigned the bus routes, saving about $5 million a year and removing 50 buses while keeping service quality (Bertsimas et al., 2019).

children.name: People, Leadership, and Culture
children.blurb: Researchers interviewed leaders in six Colorado school districts about how they first responded to AI. Some wrote informal guidelines, some banned student use, and some updated their acceptable use policies (McGuire et al., 2026).

sections.body: This part of school life is the daily and yearly work of running a school and a district, from teacher planning and grading to assessment and data, operations and finance, and people and leadership. The book describes AI entering these areas as a support for the adults who carry them out, not as a replacement for their judgement. It covers teacher planning and grading, assessment and data, operations and finance, and people and leadership as the last four chapters of the Volume. These chapters speak most directly to principals, district leaders, and board members, because the decisions in them shape the whole school. The final chapter then states the core argument of the Volume and offers a plan for the first 90 days, with a short conclusion looking back at the evidence and ahead to what may change.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The book finds that AI works in running a school when it is tied to the practical tasks adults already do, such as planning lessons, grading, watching data, and handling operations and finance. It does not work when it is treated as a substitute for the judgement of teachers, principals, district leaders, and board members, who remain responsible for the choices these chapters describe. The rule it holds to is that these chapters speak most directly to the people who run schools and districts, so the tools must serve their decisions rather than stand apart from them. The final chapter states the core argument of the Volume in full and sets out the first 90 days, which keeps the focus on a clear starting point rather than scattered adoption. A short conclusion then looks back at what the evidence shows and ahead to what may change, so the rule stays open to revision as the work develops.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages under this section fit together as the four areas of running a school, and each one is written for the person who owns that area. Teacher Planning, Grading, and Feedback is where a teacher would go for the daily work of preparing lessons and giving feedback, while Assessment, Data, and the Early Warning System is where a leader would go to see how data is used to notice students who need help. Operations, Facilities, Transportation, and Finance is for the leader or board member concerned with the physical and financial side of a school or district, and People, Leadership, and Culture is for those who shape the staff and the working climate. The final chapter then states the core argument of the Volume and sets out the first 90 days, so a principal, district leader, or board member can move from the individual pages to a plan for the whole system. A short conclusion looks back at what the evidence shows and ahead to what may change, which gives a parent or leader a sense of where the book stands and what might come next.
